item.title: Google DeepMind launches Gemini Decisions API for fast, calibrated multimodal yes/no, choice, and rubric-scoring decisions across text, images, audio, video, and PDFs [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Google DeepMind has introduced the Gemini Decisions API, powered by the Gemini Decision 1 model, enabling fast, probabilistic decision-making across multiple modalities including text, images, audio, video, and PDFs. The API can evaluate up to 1,000 yes/no, multiple choice, and rubric-scoring questions in a single pass with low latency and cost-effective pricing. The API supports combined multimodal inputs and returns confidence scores for each decision, allowing developers to route ambiguous cases to fallback systems or human reviewers. It is designed for applications such as tool selection, policy checks, model routing, and content grading, and is accessible via Google AI Studio with documentation for Python, JavaScript, and REST.

item.title: United Airlines bans AI agents from booking flights citing security risks and potential federal regulation violations [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: United Airlines announced it is prohibiting the use of artificial intelligence agents to make flight reservations on behalf of travelers due to concerns over security risks and possible violations of federal rules. The airline highlighted risks such as exposure of sensitive personal information and unintended account changes when AI tools access customer credentials. The policy update restricts AI agent access both directly on United's digital platforms and indirectly through travel agencies and aggregators. United aims to maintain control over the booking process and reduce costs associated with AI-driven flight searches, contrasting with other airlines like Southwest that have integrated AI access to flight inventories. Despite the ban, United fares remain available through flight aggregators such as Kayak, Hopper, and Google Flights, ensuring consumers can still find competitive prices.

item.title: Researcher's AI agents analyzed NASA lidar data and identified a Maya archaeological site in Mexico not listed in the official INAH register, later found to have been mapped in academic literature [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A researcher used AI agents to analyze NASA lidar data covering 1,200 km² of jungle in the Maya region, identifying a major village with distinct man-made structures that was not registered by Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH). The process took less than 72 hours from initial idea to official communication with INAH, demonstrating rapid AI-assisted archaeological discovery. Subsequent investigation revealed that the site had already been mapped in a 2025 academic study by Estrada-Belli et al., meaning the AI agents effectively rediscovered rather than newly discovered the site. The researcher documented the timeline and methodology, highlighting the potential and current limitations of AI in archaeological research and data cross-referencing.

item.title: Apple researchers present neural network approach to speed up maximum inner product search for retrieval-augmented generation, improving efficiency and accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Apple researchers introduced a method using small neural networks trained offline to accelerate maximum inner product search (MIPS), a core operation in recommendation systems and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Their approach learns typical query patterns to route searches more efficiently, reducing computational costs compared to traditional clustering methods. The technique leverages the mathematical concept of support functions and input convex neural networks to approximate the best-matching key for a query. By training separate neural networks to predict the support function and its gradient, the method achieves faster and more accurate retrieval, particularly benefiting applications where queries differ significantly from stored keys, such as short user questions versus long documents.

item.title: Atuin launches Threads to sync and search AI agent sessions across machines with end-to-end encryption [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Atuin has introduced Threads, a feature that allows users to synchronize, search, and resume AI agent sessions across multiple devices while keeping data encrypted. This enables starting a task with one AI agent on one machine and continuing it on another, preserving full context and history. Threads supports several agents including Claude Code, Codex, Pi, Omp, and OpenCode, with more planned. The system uses an encrypted sync engine that can be self-hosted or run via Atuin's servers, and captures agent sessions only if users opt in. This approach aims to make AI session histories as accessible and useful as traditional shell command histories, improving continuity and collaboration across environments.

item.title: Gilbert + Tobin CEO Sam Nickless discusses using AI to transform legal services and business operations
item.description: Sam Nickless, Partner and CEO of Gilbert + Tobin, explains how the law firm is integrating AI technologies to rethink traditional legal business models. The conversation covers the firm's approach to leveraging AI for improving efficiency and client service while adapting to evolving industry demands.

item.title: Man jailed in Turkey after using AI to scrape extensive court auction listings
item.description: A man in Turkey was imprisoned after employing an AI tool to read and collect large volumes of court auction listings. The incident highlights legal risks associated with automated data scraping in the country. Details about the charges or legal proceedings have not been disclosed.

item.title: Commerce Department finalizing AI remote access rule to block Chinese firms from accessing advanced chips via data centers in seven countries [ ! ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: The Commerce Department is finalizing a rule to prevent Chinese AI companies from remotely accessing advanced AI chips through data centers located in other countries, aiming to restrict China's access to cutting-edge AI technology. This rule is expected to expand existing semiconductor controls and cover seven additional countries, including Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand, to curb remote access and chip smuggling into China. The department is currently consulting with other government agencies before announcing the rule, which could be finalized as soon as this month. The move addresses criticism that the Commerce Department has been slow to implement policies limiting China's access to advanced AI technologies, despite opposition from major companies like Nvidia.

item.title: Investigation into Nvidia CEO's alleged ties to Chinese espionage raises concerns over leadership and AI industry impact amid $1.46 trillion market value loss [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Nvidia is under scrutiny after reports surfaced that CEO Jensen Huang had an illicit relationship linked to Chinese intelligence, involving a network that allegedly diverted $7.5 billion worth of restricted AI chips to China. The company has appointed a former US attorney to investigate potential foreign intelligence targeting, while US authorities examine the chip diversion. Nvidia denies any compromise of trade secrets or national security interests. The controversy has caused Nvidia's market value to drop by approximately $1.46 trillion over 24 trading sessions, adding uncertainty to a company central to the global AI industry. Jensen Huang's potential removal poses challenges due to his three-decade leadership, technical expertise, and political influence, with no clear successor able to immediately fill his role. The situation raises broader questions about Nvidia's future and the potential ripple effects on AI development and infrastructure commitments worldwide.

item.title: Perplexity launches Search API providing ranked web results from its index of hundreds of billions of pages with filtering and SDKs for Python and TypeScript [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Perplexity launched its Search API in September 2025, offering developers access to ranked web search results including titles, URLs, snippets, and publication dates from its continuously updated index of hundreds of billions of webpages. The API supports multiple queries per request and allows filtering by domain, language, country, and date ranges, making it suitable as a building block for agents and retrieval-augmented generation rather than a chatbot. The API includes official SDKs for Python and TypeScript and integrates with platforms like n8n, Haystack, Mastra, and Composio. Perplexity discontinued its Sonar Chat Completions API in September 2026 and now directs developers seeking cited, written answers to its Agent API, which can utilize web search as a tool.

item.title: DocSpring founder describes operating a SaaS with AI agents writing most code, detailing product development and operational challenges [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: DocSpring's founder explains how AI agents now handle much of the coding for the SaaS platform, enabling faster feature development and backlog reduction while still requiring significant human oversight. The company has expanded its document automation capabilities, including Word templates and e-signing features, with AI assisting in complex tasks like researching PDF sealing certificates. The founder manages dozens of AI sessions simultaneously to address different product areas, balancing rapid context switching and decision-making. Despite AI's role in implementation, running the business demands continuous attention to customer needs and product stability, illustrating both the opportunities and challenges of integrating AI agents into SaaS operations.

item.title: Harness explains why AI coding agents lose context after pull requests and how combining code and delivery context can maintain it [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: AI coding agents often lose track of code context once a pull request enters the delivery pipeline, missing critical evidence like build failures or deployment issues that could improve software quality. Harness highlights the need for combining code context from its Code Context Engine with delivery context from its Software Delivery Knowledge Graph to provide agents with a comprehensive understanding across the software development lifecycle. The article details how context engineering involves selecting and maintaining relevant information for AI agents beyond simple memory, emphasizing the importance of real-time indexing of code and delivery data. Harness and its partner Augment Code demonstrate that better retrieval quality significantly improves AI coding agent performance, and they are working toward an Autonomous SDLC where continuous delivery evidence informs future engineering decisions.

item.title: Google launches Gemini Decision 1, a multimodal decision model API with low latency and competitive pricing, ahead of Anthropic at AIE CODE 2026 [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: On November 11, 2026, Google announced Gemini Decision 1, a calibrated multimodal decision model capable of handling up to 1,000 questions per request with about 200ms end-to-end latency and priced at $0.10 per million input tokens. The model supports various input types including text, images, audio, video, and PDFs, and offers yes/no, multiple-choice, and rubric scoring with confidence scores for each answer. This launch was part of the second annual AIE CODE event, where Cloudflare demonstrated classifiers managing build failures and TypeSafe AI highlighted their production customers.

item.title: TypeSafe AI's Diogo Almeida urges automation with System One models at AI Engineer Code Summit; companies like Glean showcase practical Jev applications [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: At the AI Engineer Code Summit, Diogo Almeida, co-founder and CEO of TypeSafe AI and lead creator of the Jev system, advocated for widespread automation using System One models, which are faster and more reliable than traditional large language models. Almeida emphasized integrating these models directly into code to create smarter, more dependable software. Companies such as Glean demonstrated how they use Jev alongside other AI models to provide flexible, zero-shot decision-making without frequent retraining. UiPath and Workday also presented prototypes leveraging Jev for tasks like document ranking and predictive user interfaces, highlighting the model's speed and adaptability in real-world applications.

item.title: Study analyzes firm-specific AI hiring models to reveal labor market dynamics and firm differentiation in low-skill worker retention [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A recent study examines how an AI hiring platform used by large employers of low-skill workers employs firm-specific psychometric models to predict applicant retention, revealing heterogeneous firm preferences and applicant fit across contexts. The platform's ability to score all applications against each firm's model uncovers differences in how firms value traits and respond to data, offering insights for policymakers and firms to tailor interventions and investments. These findings highlight the value of platform-wide data access and model differentiation in understanding labor market behaviors and improving recruitment strategies.

item.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admits affair with alleged Chinese spy amid national security concerns; Nvidia board reportedly plans to discuss his future [ ! ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed who U.S. officials suspect is a Chinese spy. This revelation has raised national security concerns due to Megaspeed's significant purchases of Nvidia chips and alleged illegal sharing with China, amid the ongoing U.S.-China AI infrastructure competition. Reports also indicate Huang had a second affair with Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, Kimberly Powell, who reports directly to him. Following these developments, Nvidia's board is reportedly preparing to consider Huang's position, and the company's stock has declined. U.S. lawmakers are seeking to question Huang about the affair, highlighting the potential implications for technology and national security.

item.title: Reports: Nvidia board considers ousting CEO Jensen Huang amid inquiry into foreign intelligence and personal conduct [ * ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang faces potential removal as the board reportedly met to discuss his future following an inquiry into whether he was targeted by foreign intelligence and revelations of an affair involving a company executive and a possible Chinese spy. Huang, a co-founder and major shareholder with significant influence over Nvidia's operations and AI strategy, had recently been publicly supported by the board despite the investigation. His departure would underscore that even highly influential CEOs are not indispensable, despite his role in positioning Nvidia at the forefront of the AI boom and driving its market value to a peak of $5.8 trillion earlier this year.

item.title: Zarar's Blog explains how large language models interpret user intent by converting words into vectors and measuring relationships without complex math [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A blog post on Zarar's Blog details how large language models (LLMs) understand user input by transforming words into numerical vectors and assessing their relationships through vector similarity, all without requiring advanced mathematical knowledge. The explanation uses the example sentence "Do lions roar?" to illustrate how words are tokenized, converted into vectors, and compared using concepts like dot products to determine their contextual connections. The post breaks down the process into intuitive steps, describing vectors as arrows and how their directions and closeness indicate word relationships. It emphasizes that LLMs rely on relative measures of similarity to interpret meaning, making natural language processing accessible without heavy math background.

item.title: Code sandboxes isolate what agents run. What isolates what they write? [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: The article discusses the concept of code sandboxes, which are environments that isolate the execution of code by agents to enhance security and control. It raises the question of how to similarly isolate the code that these agents generate or write, highlighting the challenges and potential approaches to managing and securing dynamically produced code.

item.title: AI Inference Startups Are Quietly Buying Their Own Chips [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: The fast-growing crop of startups that lease computing capacity from cloud firms and then resell it, without spending a nickel on their own AI chips, are at a crossroads. Finding it harder to line up enough computing capacity to serve their customers, some are starting to buy their own chips, which is likely to drastically change the economics of their business. The difficulty in getting enough compute also has pushed some of these startups to look for computational resources from dozens of smaller neoclouds, which tend to have more available capacity than larger hyperscalers such as Microsoft Azure, Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud Platform. News this week of a hack of Fireworks, one of the best known of these startups, highlights the risk of that approach.

item.title: Anthropic's PE-Backed Venture, Ode, Pushes to Get Paid for AI Results [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Private equity firms and AI labs are sorting out how to charge clients and hire enough engineers for joint ventures they've launched to build custom AI tools for businesses. That comes as private equity firms are looking to the technology to boost profits, including at companies they've struggled to sell. One such team-up is Ode with Anthropic, which launched in July with $1.5 billion in capital commitments from investors including Blackstone and Hellman & Friedman. Ode currently charges most of the several dozen businesses it works with a fixed fee to develop and launch custom AI products, people familiar with the partnership say. The company lets clients retain ownership of the AI software it builds, the people said, allowing them to keep using or even sell the tools once completed without paying Ode ongoing fees. Those terms help Ode attract customers that balked at the terms offered by the team of engineers at Anthropic that embeds with enterprises, which seeks to retain ownership of the custom software it builds and license it back to customers, one of the people said. But Ode has been looking at other ways to earn more on AI projects. Some Ode executives initially proposed coinvesting in companies that were also its customers, but Blackstone's team pushed back on the idea, one of the people said. Instead, Ode decided to charge performance-based bonus fees on top of the fixed project fees, allowing it to earn more if clients hit specific financial targets. Less than 10% of Ode's clients are paying those performance-based fees, one of the people said, though Ode is aiming to grow that share. Setting the fees can be difficult because the company and its customers both need to agree on how to measure any AI-driven gains, including setting a baseline and financial or product-related goals. The fees may be negotiated once a contract is signed and Ode then does some early exploratory work and collects data, giving both sides enough information to set terms before moving on to the building phase, the people said. Ode inherited some of its business from Fractional AI, a startup founded in 2024 that the venture acquired in May for an undisclosed sum. Fractional already worked mostly with private equity-backed companies to automate tasks and build custom AI software, and Fractional co-founders Chris Taylor and Eddie Siegel became Ode's CEO and chief technology officer, respectively. One of those clients, risk and compliance software company LogicGate, paid a fixed fee in the low seven figures for a project that began under Fractional last summer and finished this fall, said LogicGate CEO Diego Panama. (LogicGate's backers include growth equity firm PSG, which led the company's $113 million funding round in 2021.) Ode engineers built a custom agent that shortened LogicGate's client onboarding from 120 days to 90 days or less. LogicGate received full intellectual property ownership and training to run the tool independently, Panama said, and it subsequently began selling the agent to other businesses and has signed several deals. The agent is set to launch publicly at the end of the month. Around half of Ode's clients are software or business services companies, while the rest come from industrial and other sectors. Its client base is split roughly equally between portfolio companies of Ode's backers, including at least six Blackstone companies, and other businesses. All of the Blackstone portfolio companies working with Ode currently pay fixed fees, including accounting firm Citrin Cooperman, where Ode engineers built a new onboarding system, similar to the work they did at LogicGate. Blackstone typically sets targets to improve earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization in a specific division when evaluating how an AI project is working. Other AI services firms are experimenting with similar fee structures. Hyde, backed by Bain Capital Ventures and General Catalyst, launched last year and helps businesses build custom AI models using their own data. Clients then own the customer models and can run them themselves or pay Hyde to host them. Hyde typically assigns two engineers to work with clients for around four weeks per project, charging for that work plus a recurring fee for using its software platform. (Clients also pay for compute based on usage.) Around half its contracted revenue includes a portion of fees tied to results-its fee for an automotive client, for example, is tied to whether agents meet certain car sales goals. Hyde CEO Anirudh Sanga said demand for Hyde's services has roughly doubled monthly for the past three months. At the same time, a shortage of engineers is limiting how much business AI services firms can take on. Anthropic itself has sought to address the shortage, announcing a $100 million effort last month to train 10,000 deployment engineers at customer and partner companies by the end of next year. Upstart AI services firms are also competing with major tech firms for talent. Microsoft in July committed $2.5 billion to its Microsoft Frontier Co. with the aim of placing 6,000 engineers inside enterprise customers, partnering with consultancies like Accenture and EY. As of November 2025, Fractional had an annual revenue run rate of over $12 million. At the time of the May acquisition, it was generating around $30 million in ARR, which has since nearly tripled, according to people familiar with the matter. But Ode is being selective about the clients it takes on because it doesn't have enough engineers to handle all potential business, one of the people said, though it has enough demand for at least two to three times its current workload. OpenAI Deployment Co. has faced similar constraints. The venture, backed by TPG and other investment firms including Brookfield Asset Management and Bain Capital, has sought to hire more engineers to expand available capacity. Ode has made several acquihires and acquisitions since launching, including one of Casper Studios, which designed specialized AI products using Claude. Ode remains open to exploring more deals, a person familiar with the venture said, but is looking to expand its services or geographic reach instead of simply adding more people. Hyde, for its part, isn't currently seeking acquisitions, but it has declined several takeover offers, Sanga said, mostly from large companies looking to quickly establish their own AI deployment team. Fintech and Crypto Startups to Watch Each year, The Information picks 50 startups that have the potential to be breakout stars. This time around, our fintech and crypto category featured new twists on trading and betting and startups positioned to benefit from growth in emerging areas like agentic payments. There's Fomo, a viral trading app that plans to branch out from memecoins to tokenized stocks, and Catalyst, a startup offering agents that help people trade across venues like prediction markets and crypto exchanges. On the payments side, Natural is offering bank accounts for AI agents, while stablecoin-backed card provider Kast is expanding beyond retail customers by courting merchants. item.title: Anthropic, Others Warn of AI Acceleration [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: In recent weeks, my colleagues and I have been trying our hand at being venture capitalists: today, the end result of that process is our annual list of the 50 most promising startups of this year, published today. We've had a pretty good track record in past years: AI startups we've previously highlighted include OpenRouter, when the model-routing startup was valued at $500 million; Cursor, when the coding agent was valued at $400 million; and Perplexity, when the AI-powered search engine was valued at $150 million. OpenRouter was recently acquired by Stripe for more than $7 billion, Cursor in August was acquired by SpaceX for $60 billion, and Perplexity was most recently raising at a more than $30 billion valuation. Each year, however, it gets more difficult to pick promising AI startups that fall within our requirements of having raised less than $100 million and being valued less than $1 billion. These days, it feels like the moment any young AI company has a hint of revenue traction, investors are all over them. Still, we've managed to uncover a number of under-the-radar gems in this year's list. In fact, we had trouble whittling down the entrants for our AI infrastructure and security categories, which included everything from companies that help developers train their models using multiple cloud providers to those that use AI to protect employees' devices. Such companies have become even more important as the rate of AI-powered cyberattacks have increased.-Stephanie Palazzolo Now, onto today's column... AI researchers that focus on ensuring AI doesn't harm humans have reason to be a little rattled. Two recent reports suggest AI is advancing even more quickly than previously thought, and that's increased these safety researchers' worries that AI will escape human control to wreak havoc.

item.title: Introducing The Information's 50 Most Promising Startups of 2026
item.description: As artificial intelligence changes how companies get hacked, investors are paying up for startups that promise to keep defenders ahead. That dynamic shaped this year's The Information 50, our annual list of the most promising startups. For the first time, our list includes a category devoted solely to security, and it holds some of the list's biggest bets. Two of the four most highly valued companies in this seventh edition of the list are security startups valued at more than $1 billion apiece, and six of the security firms are run by Israelis, which have a long history of breakout hits in this field. At a time when many people use AI to research new companies, our reporters didn't use AI to find candidates. They just had good ol' fashioned conversations with dozens of founders and investors-including many that pointed us to startups they missed out on-and collected hard data on revenue and growth rates at the companies. You can view the list here, and join our conference call for The Information subscribers at 12pm PT / 3pm ET to discuss the list with several of the founders whose companies are on it.

item.title: Amazon and Google Win Big From Anthropic IPO [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: If you're looking for a cheaper way of getting exposure to Anthropic than buying the stock directly, consider Amazon or Google. Anthropic's updated IPO filing on Tuesday shows just how many shares each of those two tech giants will own in Anthropic, along with how much money they're making on their early investments in the AI firm. Neither tech giant will own voting shares in Anthropic, so antitrust cops won't have to worry about their influence over its management. But their stakes are significant. In theory, Amazon could own around 20% of Anthropic's outstanding shares. But because of a self-imposed ownership cap, Amazon won't hold more than 12% of Anthropic. The rest of its holdings are convertible notes that can convert to equity over time. Regardless, Amazon's economic return is pretty damn good. Forgetting about the ownership cap for a minute, Amazon's entire 20%-or-so stake would be worth about $258 billion at the midpoint of Anthropic's proposed IPO pricing range. That's from an investment totaling around $18.6 billion. (Anthropic's final IPO price may well end up higher than the preliminary range, a Financial Times report tonight suggests).
